rows.description: A child changes answers to whatever seems to please the teacher and looks anxiously at faces for a sign; approval is a strong reward but can crowd out honest thought.
Adults watch a teenager take a dangerous dare and struggle to tell bravery from need for approval. Real courage serves a value, while recklessness serves an audience.

rows.subtype: Feeling like a fraud in a top college [Actor]
rows.description: A student admitted to a prestigious institute believes they got in by luck and that everyone will soon find out; success is discounted while comparison with others is harsh.

rows.subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
rows.description: The new hire stays late, avoids asking questions and quietly studies at night to catch up. Not asking for help feels safer than exposing ignorance, but it slows learning.
A child who takes longer with reading calls themselves dumb and stops trying; a single label replaces a specific skill that can be practised.

rows.subtype: Excited, eager and worried mixed together [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager before a trip, exam or first job interview may feel eager and anxious at once, with the same racing heart. Labelling it as excitement can turn nervous energy into readiness.

rows.subtype: Hiding behind a parent at a party [Actor]
rows.description: A child clings to a parent's leg and refuses to greet anyone; staying away from the scary thing feels like relief, and gentle nearness helps more than pushing.

rows.subtype: Approach: puts off an unpleasant task by doing something easy [Pitfall]
rows.description: A boy with a hard maths worksheet suddenly tidies his bookshelf and sharpens every pencil. The task he fears stays untouched.
A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A parent sees a child stressed by tiny errors and is torn between pride and worry. Shares their own mistakes and shows that being good enough is fine, without shaming the child's high standards.

A young adult researches a project for weeks, refining an outline that is never good enough to begin. Preparing feels productive but is a way of postponing the risk of being judged.
